theme: Jonah flees; the storm; the great fish
readingInstruction: Read Jonah 1:1-2:10. A reluctant prophet runs from God’s call, a storm threatens the ship, and a great fish swallows Jonah. Read the story as the Bible tells it: with humor, irony, and a surprising ending.
settingTheScene: Jonah son of Amittai was a prophet in the northern kingdom during Jeroboam II (see 2 Kings 14:25). God sends him to Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, the empire that will later destroy Israel. For an Israelite, this was the last place he would want to go. The book is unusual among the prophets: it is mostly a story about the prophet rather than his sermons. And it shows that God’s mercy reaches those whom Israel considered enemies.
observation: “Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, for their evil has come up before me” (1:2).
“But Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the LORD” (1:3).
“But the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea” (1:4).
“But Jonah had gone down into the inner part of the ship and had lain down and was fast asleep” (1:5).
“I am a Hebrew, and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land” (1:9).
“Pick me up and hurl me into the sea; then the sea will quiet down for you” (1:12).
“Then the men feared the LORD exceedingly, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows” (1:16).
“And the LORD appointed a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights” (1:17).
interpretation:
The book begins with a command and a flight. Jonah is told to go to Nineveh, and he goes in the opposite direction. The text notes the movement: he goes down to Joppa, down into the ship, down into the hold. Every step is downward. When we run from God, we go down.

The irony is rich. The pagan sailors are devout and the prophet is asleep. They cry out to their gods, while the one man who knows the true God is unconscious. The captain says to him, “Arise, call out to your god!” using the same words God had said to Jonah in 1:2. When Jonah confesses, “I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land,” the irony is complete. He says he fears the LORD, yet he is running from him. His words are right, but his life is not.

The sailors are more compassionate than Jonah. They try to row back to land rather than throw him overboard. They pray that they will not be guilty of innocent blood. And when they do throw him in and the sea grows calm, they fear the LORD and offer a sacrifice. The pagans are converted, and the prophet is sinking.

Then God appoints a great fish. The fish is not a punishment but an act of rescue. Jonah was drowning, and God saves him. Chapter 2 is Jonah’s prayer from inside the fish, and it is a psalm of thanksgiving. He describes sinking into the deep, with seaweed wrapped around his head. “I called out to the LORD, out of my distress, and he answered me.” He recalls that he was cast “into the heart of the seas.” He confesses: “Those who pay regard to vain idols forsake their hope of steadfast love.” And he concludes: “Salvation belongs to the LORD!”

The prayer is theologically right, but notice that it contains no repentance for running away. Jonah thanks God for deliverance but does not yet say that he will obey. The fish then vomits him onto dry land. Salvation is God’s work from beginning to end.
connection: Jesus said, “An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:39-40). Jesus slept in a boat during a storm and calmed it (Mark 4:38-39). He is the one who was thrown into the sea of judgment so that others might be saved. “Salvation belongs to the LORD” is fulfilled in Jesus, whose name means “The LORD saves.”
application:
Where are you running from something God has asked of you? Name it.

Notice the grace of God in the “appointed fish” in your life, rescues you did not recognize at the time.

Pray Jonah’s last line, “Salvation belongs to the LORD,” as a statement of trust.
prayerPrompts: Confess where you have run from God.
Thank him for pursuing you and rescuing you.
Ask him to help you go where he sends.
